nodes.label: Spring local Profile
nodes.rationale: In-memory H2 in PostgreSQL mode, no Postgres and no password, port 8080 bound to 0.0.0.0 so the phone can reach it, Google client-ids preset. The database lives only while the process runs — every start is a clean seed, deliberately, so no junk accumulates. Must be launched from the repo root because AttachmentServiceImpl resolves files relative to backend/files.

nodes.label: LocalSeeder Test Data
nodes.rationale: Runs only when app.local.seed=true, a property present only in the local profile, so it cannot fire on the server by accident. Phones, emails and measurements are left empty on purpose because on the live API those are PII served without authorisation. Photos are generated on the fly with deterministic names so reruns reuse the same files.

nodes.label: LAN IP In EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL
nodes.rationale: The phone must target the computer's LAN IP, not localhost. EXPO_PUBLIC_* are inlined into the bundle at build time, so editing .env without restarting Metro changes nothing — the most common cause of 'the app loads no data' is a stale IP after a Wi-Fi change.

nodes.label: Dev Firewall Exposure
nodes.rationale: Inbound 8080 (backend) and 8081 (Metro) are opened for the Private profile only. Because SecurityConfig lets anyone in, the local backend is visible to everyone on a shared network — the data is fake and in-memory, but the rules should be removed after work.

nodes.label: H2 Console And open-in-view Pitfalls
nodes.rationale: spring.h2.console.enabled=true adds a servlet after which Spring Security cannot decide whether the SecurityConfig patterns are Spring MVC patterns and startup fails, so the console is off. open-in-view=false breaks /casting-user/web because CastingUser.photos is lazy and serialised outside the transaction (500) — meaning the production backend depends on that setting too, and it must be changed together with the backend developer.
